summary.text: A seamount is a large undersea landform, typically an extinct volcano, that rises from the ocean floor without reaching the surface.
Seamounts are so numerous that they form one of the most common marine ecosystems, attracting plankton, corals, fish and marine mammals.
More than 14,500 have been identified, but only a few have been studied in detail, and ships have even collided with uncharted ones.

items.prompt: If every known seamount were gathered into one place, about how big would the landform be?

options.label: The size of a large city
The size of a small island
The size of Europe
The size of the Moon

items.explain: All known seamounts collected into one area would make a landform the size of Europe.

items.prompt: Fishing fleets often work the waters right above seamounts. Why?

options.label: The water there is always warmer
Currents and the raised peak draw in sea life
Nets never snag on the rocky bottom
Sunlight reaches all the way to the summit

items.explain: Interactions with currents and their elevated position attract plankton, corals and fish, and many seamounts support extensive fisheries.

items.prompt: As a seamount ages, material seeping into it puts pressure on its sides. What can that eventually lead to?

options.label: Landslides that can set off huge tsunamis
A sudden rise until it becomes an island
A steady leak of fresh water into the sea
A slow change into a coral reef

items.explain: Pressure on the flanks causes landslides that can generate massive tsunamis, the greatest danger from seamounts.

items.prompt: A big seamount grows up to the surface, waves wear its summit level, and then it sinks again. What is it now called?

options.label: An atoll
A trench
A ridge
A guyot

items.explain: After they subside below the surface, such flat-top seamounts are called guyots or tablemounts.

items.prompt: The Emperor Seamounts northwest of Hawaii were built by volcanoes millions of years ago. What has happened to them since?

options.label: They have grown into new islands
They have melted back into magma
They have sunk far below sea level
They have drifted into the Arctic

items.explain: Formed by volcanism millions of years ago, the Emperor Seamounts have since subsided far below sea level.

items.prompt: Why are most seamounts found on ocean crust near mid-ocean ridges, mantle plumes and island arcs?

options.label: Currents pile sediment there
Most of them began as volcanoes
The water there is shallowest
Coral grows fastest in those spots

items.explain: Most seamounts are volcanic in origin, so they tend to sit near ridges, mantle plumes and island arcs.

paragraphs.heading: Mountains that stay underwater
paragraphs.text: A seamount is a large landform that rises from the ocean floor but never reaches the surface, so it is not an island. Most are extinct volcanoes that rise steeply, usually 100 to 4,000 m above the seafloor. Oceanographers define one as a stand-alone, cone-shaped rise of at least 1,000 m with a small summit area. Their peaks are often hundreds to thousands of meters below the surface, which puts them in the deep sea.

paragraphs.heading: Born from volcanoes
paragraphs.text: Most seamounts are volcanic, so they tend to sit on oceanic crust close to mid-ocean ridges, island arcs and mantle plumes. Those close to ridges and plate boundaries are built by what is called decompression melting of upper-mantle rock. A few, like the Christmas Island Seamount Province near Australia, are harder to explain. Over geologic time the biggest seamounts may reach the surface, where waves wear the summit flat. Once they sink back down, these flat-topped seamounts are called guyots or tablemounts.

paragraphs.heading: How many there are
paragraphs.text: More than 14,500 seamounts have been identified, and 9,951 seamounts plus 283 guyots have been mapped, yet scientists have studied only a few closely. The oceans also hold more than 80,000 smaller knolls, ridges and hills under 1,000 m tall. Gathered into one place, all known seamounts would make a landform the size of Europe. They are most plentiful in the North Pacific, where seamounts and guyots cover 4.39% of the seafloor, while the Arctic holds just 16 seamounts and not a single guyot.

paragraphs.heading: Chains under the sea
paragraphs.text: Seamounts often come in groups, like drowned archipelagos. A classic case is the Emperor Seamounts, which continue the Hawaiian Islands thousands of kilometers to the northwest from the island of Hawaii. Volcanism built them millions of years ago, and they have since sunk far below sea level. The Pacific has the most seamount chains and the longest ones. Some seamounts are still active, such as Kamaʻehuakanaloa, formerly called Lōʻihi, in the Hawaiian Islands.

paragraphs.heading: Gathering places for life
paragraphs.text: There are so many seamounts that they rank among the world's most common marine ecosystems. The way they meet underwater currents, and their raised position in the water, draw in plankton, corals, fish and marine mammals. Commercial fishing has noticed this, and many seamounts support large fisheries. There are ongoing worries about the harm fishing does, with well-documented declines in stocks such as the orange roughy. Bottom trawling, which scrapes whole ecosystems off seamounts, does 95% of the ecological damage.

paragraphs.heading: Hidden hazards
paragraphs.text: Many seamounts are still not properly studied or even mapped, and bathymetry and satellite altimetry are two technologies helping to close that gap. Naval ships have run into uncharted seamounts: Muirfield Seamount is named after the ship that hit it in 1973. The biggest danger, though, is a flank collapse. As a seamount ages, material pushing into it presses on its sides and can set off landslides able to cause massive tsunamis.
